I have organized more than two hundred panels, and I can tell you a secret. The best panelists are not the ones with the best English. They are the ones with a clear point of view. Before every forum, I call each panelist and ask one question: what do you want the audience to remember? If they can answer in one sentence, the panel will work. If they cannot, it does not matter how fluent they are. My other advice is simple. Do not read your opening remarks. Look at the audience, speak slowly, and finish on time. Nobody ever complained that a panelist was too short.

The first time a conference in London invited me, I said no. I told them I was too busy, but the truth was different. I was afraid that somebody would ask a question I could not understand. Two years later, they invited me again. This time I said yes, and I prepared for six weeks. I rehearsed my opening remarks every morning, and I asked a colleague to play the moderator. On the day, I was nervous for the first two minutes. After that, I forgot about my English and talked about my work. A partner from a fund came to me after the panel, and that conversation became my biggest client.
